And the deeper problem your correction exposes: **these are one-shot origin stories — launch capital, not an engine.** The story bank gives us maybe 8 weeks at this cadence, then it's dry. A 70% engine needs formats that are *repeatable without input*. From his own data, only three qualify:

1. **Hiring/team posts** — n=37, avg 110, max 321, and generable from their public job listings without asking him. His most repeatable proven format by far.
2. **Radical ops takes with receipts** — fired-customers genre, feeds off the call reservoir.
3. **Reactive takes on big AI/insurance news** — infinitely renewable. His old ones flopped at 37, but those were news-desk voice; first-person with a hard opinion is a different animal. Needs testing, small quota first.

Nothing else in his history is both proven and input-free. That's the real content engine question.

Next move: I re-cut batch 1 as a true week-1 under the quota math — 6 engagement (hiring + radical + best 3 stories), 2 BOFU, 1 TPA — and verify whether Cozmo has live job listings to fuel format #1. Starting on the listings check now unless you redirect.

### Ansh  
One girl solved what NINE PhD students couldn't crack in 4 months

She is my co-founder now, @Nuha Hashem

In my first year of university, I joined a research group.

Everyone else was a PhD student from Stanford or Berkeley. I was the youngest one in the room.

One problem had been stuck for 4 months. Nine very smart people. No progress.

Then Nuha joined. Quiet, fresh from Egypt, didn't say much in the first meeting.

Three days later... solved.

That day taught me something I've used ever since. Talent shows up in work, not in introductions.

Years later, in 2021, I quit my consulting job to start a company. Everyone told me to find a co-founder with a famous resume.

I called the girl from that room instead.

A resume tells you what someone was allowed to do. I'd seen what she could actually do.

She was months away from finishing her PhD in the US. I asked her to walk away from it and build with me.

All in, or NOTHING.

She picked all in.

Since then we built:

- a banking app
- then a pivot
- then another pivot
- through a war
- and now Cozmo (YC W22), AI that handles insurance claims

She rebuilt our core technology more times than I can count. Usually while I was out selling, with no idea how much was on fire behind the scenes.

People ask me how to pick a co-founder. One answer.

Don't pick a resume. Pick the person you watched do the impossible when nobody was grading them.

P.S. Where did you find YOUR co-founder? I collect these stories.

What the humanizer changed, and why:

1. **The three resume aphorisms became one.** "Talent shows up in work, not in introductions" and "A resume tells you what someone was allowed to do / I'd seen what she could actually do" and "Don't pick a resume, pick the person..." were the same contrast three times — a stacked symmetric-pair cluster, which is the single most reliable LLM signature. Live in your Safari. The Charlie Hills version:

> Google will pay SpaceX $920,000,000 every month
>
> Not once. Every month. For 32 months
>
> 32 months, about 110,000 GPUs, just under $30 billion to use somebody else's computers.
>
> And it's Google doing the renting. The company that built half the plumbing the internet runs on.

**What his principle changed** (structure, not words): I deleted every sentence that interpreted a fact for the reader. "The part I can't get over is who's doing the renting" told them what to feel — now the sentence just states that it's Google and stops. "Which tells you where the money actually sits" told them what to conclude — gone; the model-vs-machine contrast now lands the point without narrating it. And the gold-rush metaphor was the neat bow he warns about; it's replaced with a detail that leaves the thought slightly open.

We had **no** Charlie Hills anti-AI skill in the repo — the `product/skills/charlie/` suite is his post-writer/voice-builder tooling, which only handles voice absence patterns. So I wrote [stay-human-charlie.md](../Snowball/product/skills/stay-human-charlie.md) from his actual published principle, structured as a four-step pass to run *after* the blader humanizer: blader fixes vocabulary, this fixes shape. It's product-level, so every client gets it.

Sources: [Charlie Hills on humanizing AI writing](https://substack.com/@charliehills/note/c-298181464), [his voice-extraction method](https://substack.com/@charliehills/note/c-206387723), [Charlie Hills on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/charlie-hills/).

### Alfred  
The Charlie repo is 17 skills, sir — a full production suite, not just writing. What's in it and what's actually worth using:

**Immediately valuable for Cozmo:**
- **post-scorer** — scores a draft against the client's *own* real post history (pulls via Apify, or falls back to Charlie's benchmark: 1,872 avg engagement across 500 posts). This is the one that would have settled every "will this work?" argument with Alok on the call. We can run it on all 10 posts before he sees them.
- **hook-generator** — 6 hooks per topic on a fixed formula: two lines, ≤40 characters each, line 2 contradicts line 1, always a digit or an "I" statement, across 6 angles (number-led, contrarian, transformation, authority steal, admission, future shock). ---

## The philosophy, in his own framing

From the README: *"The complete set of Claude skills behind Charlie Hills' content system. 350k+ followers across LinkedIn, Instagram, Substack, X and YouTube. 100m+ views per year. **All running through one system that starts with the newsletter and flows out to every other channel.**"*

Two structural beliefs sit underneath it:

**1. Voice is the foundation, and it is a file.** *"Every skill reads shared context. The `voice-builder` skill is the foundation. Every other skill checks it first (via `about-me.md` and `voice.md`) before drafting a line."* The instruction is blunt: *"Run `voice-builder` first. Every other skill needs `about-me.md` and `voice.md` to work properly."*

**2. The newsletter is the source.** His dependency diagram puts `newsletter-voice` directly beneath voice-builder, labelled *"the source every piece comes from"* — and everything else (profile, LinkedIn posts, video, analytics, community, standalone) branches off *below* it. He writes long-form first, and every channel is downstream repurposing.

---

## How the skills are wired

```
voice-builder (about-me.md + voice.md)
        │
newsletter-voice (newsletter-voice.md) ← "the source every piece comes from"
        │
   ┌────┴────┬─────────┬──────────┬──────────┬───────────┐
 Profile  LinkedIn   Video   Analytics   Community   Standalone
```

**Voice foundation:** voice-builder, newsletter-voice
**LinkedIn:** profile-optimizer, post-writer, graphic-designer, post-formatter, hook-generator, post-scorer, content-matrix, niche-research, gemini-infographic, gemini-carousel, quote-post
**Instagram:** reels-scripting · **YouTube:** youtube-thumbnail · **Community:** pinned-comment · **Analytics:** analytics-dashboard

---

## The mechanics worth reading in full

**voice-builder** — a two-batch `AskUserQuestion` interview (max 4 questions per call) plus 3-5 writing samples. It produces `voice.md` with sections for tone, sentence rhythm, hook patterns, how I open, how I close, and critically **"What this voice never does"** — and his rule on that section: *"Every item must be backed by absence across the samples,"* drawn *"from observation, not from a generic banned-words template."* That is the opposite of how I've been working — I've been applying banned-word lists; he derives them from evidence.

**post-scorer** — the most rigorous skill in the repo. It scrapes 100 posts via Apify actor `apimaestro/linkedin-profile-posts`, then computes **engagement = reactions + (comments × 3)**, isolates the **top 10%** and the **bottom 10%**, and extracts hook types, average word count, format distribution, CTA patterns, topic clusters and sentence rhythm from them. It then scores a draft 1-10 on five criteria: hook strength, voice match, value density, structure/format, publish readiness. Two lines matter most: *"Score 8+ only if the hook type matches a pattern in their top 10%"* and, under publish readiness, *"Did the user actually write this or does it read like unedited AI output?"* Fallback benchmark if you have no data: **Charlie's own — 1,872 avg engagement, 500 posts analysed.**

**hook-generator** — fixed formula: two lines, **40 characters max each**, line 2 contradicts or undercuts line 1, at least one "I"/"How I" statement, a digit where possible. Six angles: number-led, contrarian, personal transformation, authority steal, admission, future shock.

**post-formatter** — five named frameworks: **PAS** (Problem→Agitation→Solution), **AIDA** (Attention→Interest→Desire→Action), **BAB** (Before→After→Bridge), **STAR** (Situation→Task→Action→Result), **SLAY** (Story→Lesson→Actionable advice→You). Hard constraints: 200-250 words, 20 lines max, blank line between sentences, closes with "Repost if" / "Repost this" / "If this helped, repost" plus the recycle symbol. He also draws a clean line: *"post-formatter applies a strict framework. post-writer drafts in the user's voice without framework constraints."*

**content-matrix** — Justin Welsh style, pillars × 8 formats = 32+ ideas. This is the one update since launch (20 May): surface-aware output — interactive chart on chat surfaces, **saved as `content-matrix-YYYY-MM-DD.md` on Claude Code** — because *"that renders as monospace plain text and makes a 5×8 grid hard to scan."*

**gemini-infographic** — described plainly as *"The whiteboard style that pulled 480k impressions from 3 posts."*

---

## The house style he enforces on every skill

From CONTRIBUTING.md, applied repo-wide:
- British English, "ise" not "ize"
- **Short sentences. No em dashes. No semicolons.**
- **Never use: "leverage" (as a verb), "deep dive", "unlock", "game-changer", "groundbreaking"**
- Every skill starts with `## CRITICAL: Auto-start on load` — *"Do not summarise. Start immediately."*
- Use `AskUserQuestion` for inputs rather than typing questions
- SKILL.md under 500 lines; overflow goes to `references/`
- A `## Rules` section at the bottom of every skill with "never"/"always" phrasing
- Any skill that writes a file must state the exact filename and location; any skill depending on another's output must check for it first

**Prerequisites:** `APIFY_API_TOKEN` (post-scorer, reels-scripting), `GOOGLE_AI_API_KEY` (reels-scripting). The image skills *"output ready-to-paste prompts. You run them in a separate Gemini chat with Create Image enabled. No API key needed."*

**Install (his preferred path):** `/plugin marketplace add charlie947/social-media-skills` then `/plugin install social-media-skills`.

**Licence:** MIT. *"Use these however you like. If they help you, a link back to the newsletter is appreciated."*

Source: [charlie947/social-media-skills](https://github.com/charlie947/social-media-skills) · [MarTech AI newsletter](https://charliehills.substack.com)

### Alfred  
Here it is, sir — his philosophy, in his words, from his newsletter and his own posts. No additions from me.

---

## Why post at all

> **"Content creation and brand building are long-term games. If you are in this for a quick buck, this is not the game you should be playing."**

The purpose he states: **"to build something that compounds. Something that fuels the rest of your career and business."**

And the brutal premise underneath it:

> **"No one cares who you are. Unless you are already famous, a recognised industry leader, or someone with an audience elsewhere, LinkedIn owes you nothing."**

He frames the platform as a **"predictable growth engine"** for B2B, and opens with the urgency: *"By the time you finish reading, LinkedIn will have added ~1,000 new members."* His own growth **stayed invisible for six months** before it compounded.

---

## What to post about

**The failure mode he names:**

> **"They try to speak to everyone. They drift between topics. They change direction every few weeks based on what performs. The result is attention without association."**

That last phrase is the thesis: being seen without being *associated with anything* is worthless.

**The structure he prescribes:** 3-5 content pillars → a content matrix (each idea explored from multiple angles) → specific topics drawn from lived experience.

**The 70/20/10 funnel ratio:**
- **70% Awareness (TOFU)** — *"quick, practical wins that solve immediate pain"*: cheat-sheets, swipe files, myth-busting
- **20% Authority (MOFU)** — story-driven, showing the craft: *"Pull back the curtain, share the 'why'"*
- **10% Conversion (BOFU)** — *only when trust is banked*, treated as **"genuine help, not spammy intrusion"**

---

## The four beliefs that drive everything

**1. Your lived experience is the moat.**
> **"Your moat now and going forward is your lived experience. That is the one thing AI cannot easily replace."**
> **"If a stranger could have posted it, delete it."**

**2. Posting isn't the job.**
> **"Posting is not the job. Distribution is."**
He runs a **60-minute engagement circuit**: warm the feed before posting, publish with intent, then convert impressions into conversations by commenting.

**3. Consistency is the whole edge.**
> **"If you post consistently. You are already ahead of 99% of users."**

**4. Personality is non-negotiable.**
> **"Visibility without personality is noise."**

On studying other creators: learn **"the mechanics, not the personality"** — take the structure, keep your own voice.

---

## On automation (the part most relevant to what we do)

> **"The founder doing every task is the ceiling. I was the ceiling."**

He automated 80% and kept exactly one thing:

> **"I am the final gate, and only the final gate."**
> **"I read it, I feel it, I approve it. That last yes is the one thing I keep."**

How he got there: **"I spent months feeding Claude my tastes, my standards, the way I judge whether a post is worth publishing."** And on what people actually lack: **"What you lack now is ideas and a system that turns them into posts worth reading."**

---

## What his own top posts actually do

From our scrape of his 50 most recent — his highest performers (2,700 / 2,600 / 2,364 engagement) are all the same shape: **a number in the hook, a curated resource list, and links.** "Anthropic won't send you this list", "Claude Code has 93 commands. Here are the 16 worth learning first", "I've already replaced 12 tools in my workflow this year."

Every one closes with the same two moves: **"Repost ♻️ to help someone in your network"** and a **P.S. question** ("Which one are you using most?"), often followed by a newsletter P.S.S. He practises exactly the 70% awareness content he preaches — practical wins, saveable, no personal storytelling.

---

### Alfred  
Real answer, sir, with the reasoning exposed.

## The two pillars are not parallel. One multiplies the other.

DMs are the only thing that touches the P&L directly. Content almost never produces a customer on its own — you said it yourself on Alok's call, and our own data backs it: **11% of his 1,695 buyers have posted in 30 days.** They're not scrolling for vendors.

But here's the mechanic that matters: **the DM is the ask, the profile is the credential check.** Every buyer who gets a message opens the profile before deciding whether to reply — and more importantly, *how* to reply. A cold DM from a blank profile is a vendor. The same DM from someone whose feed shows a founder who rebuilt a workflow in 2 days is a peer. Same message, different reply rate, different power dynamic in the meeting that follows.

So content isn't a second channel. **It's the conversion rate on the first one.** That's why we run them together, and why profile optimization is worth more per hour than any single post.

## What content actually accumulates

Beyond that multiplier, four things — none of them customers:

1. **Talent.** Alok's own data: hiring posts averaged 110 reactions, max 321. He told us he ships something new weekly and announces none of it. Engineers follow founders for a year before they apply. This is the highest-ROI use of a founder feed and almost nobody runs it deliberately.
2. **Capital.** Investors don't discover you in a feed, they *track* you in one. Watching someone execute in public for six months is diligence that costs them nothing.
3. **Surface area.** Partnerships, press, podcasts, acquisition conversations — all arrive as inbound to people who are legible. You can't manufacture luck, you can only widen the aperture.
4. **Compounding.** Charlie's framing is right: *"build something that compounds."* His growth was invisible for six months. Anyone who quits at month three is paying the cost and collecting none of the return.

## The trick nobody says out loud

**You write for an audience that will never buy, so that a handful who never engage reach a conclusion.**

The many — founders, engineers, tech people — give you reach and reactions. They'll never be customers. The few — those 1,695 — give you revenue and will never like a post.

Content aimed at the many is what *produces the artifact* that persuades the few. Reach is not the goal; reach is what makes the artifact exist and stay visible. That's why engagement metrics matter and simultaneously don't.

## So what do you post about?

Not the company. **Nobody has ever cared about your company.** Three things earn a stranger's attention:

- **Stories only they could tell.** Charlie's rule is the sharpest test I've read: *"If a stranger could have posted it, delete it."* Lived experience is the only thing that can't be regenerated by a model.
- **News they'd read anyway, plus a take.** You buy attention with utility and repay it with judgment. The take is what converts a reader into a follower — without it you're a wire service.
- **Resources they'd save.** Highest save rate, fastest follower growth, weakest association. Use sparingly or you become a link account.

And the one thing to never post: **education about your own industry.** Alok's five worst posts ever were industry takes, 19-41 reactions, against 100-582 for stories. Buyers already know their industry. Teaching them is condescension dressed as thought leadership.

**My five-question filter for any idea:** Could only they have written it? Would a stranger finish it? Does it make one person think "this team is unusually good"? Is it about the reader's world, not the poster's company? Would anyone save it?

## The honest tension in what we're currently doing

Our 70/30 split optimizes for reach among founders. For Alok, **founders are not buyers.** So most of his feed serves talent, capital, and the credential check — not his stated #1 goal, customers. That's a defensible trade, and it's exactly why the 20% BOFU slots and the profile rebuild carry the revenue weight while the rest carries everything else.

Worth saying that plainly to him, and worth pricing it that way to the next YC founder: **we don't sell reach. We sell the reason a buyer says yes to the DM, and the compound asset that keeps working after.**

### Alfred  
Fixed at the root, sir, and verified in the live page — all ten images now render at their true aspect ratio, zero distortion.

**What was actually wrong — my processing, not the API.** To keep the payload under the limit I'd been palette-quantizing everything to 160-200 colours. That's fine for flat vector art, but it destroys photographs: it forces millions of tones into a few hundred, which is exactly the banding and the acid over-saturation you spotted. Then I compounded it by cropping the 2006 photo to `width = height × 0.8`, which sliced the computer, keyboard and monitor clean out of frame and left only the two of them.

**The fix, permanently:**

1. **Photographs now ship as high-quality JPEG (q86-88), never palette-quantized.** I taught the push tool to accept `.jpg`/`.jpeg` and send them with the proper `data:image/jpeg` prefix, which the API already supported — I just wasn't using it. The results are both sharper *and* smaller: the Forbes photo went from 440KB of crushed PNG to 178KB of clean JPEG.
2. **The computer photo is uncropped.** Full frame at 1080×810 — Alok, his brother, the keyboard, the Philips monitor, the 2006 date stamp, all of it.
3. **Photo-like renders** (the isometric city, the data infographic, the flight shot) also moved to JPEG. **True flat art** (pixel graphics, tweet cards) stays PNG at full 256 colours.
4. **Total payload dropped from 3.1MB to 2.1MB** while quality went up across the board — so there's now real headroom instead of me squeezing pixels to fit.

The Forbes and Future 100 photos now sit at proper 4:5 and near-square framing with both faces intact, and every image passed the programmatic ratio check.

## Blockers before I arm it

1. **He's connected twice** — `8e1cp_oB…` and `fdREXgQN…`, same profile `alokhk`, created 34 seconds apart. If anything ever iterates accounts, he double-posts. One should be deleted; I haven't touched it since it's his asset.

3. **The cadence has a flaw worth naming.** 17-hour intervals land these at 10am, 3am, 8pm, 1pm, 6am, 11pm, 4pm, 9am, 2am, 7pm SF. **Half the batch publishes overnight.** That's inherent to a 17-hour gap and it was the intent — but it means week one is testing *time of day* as much as format. Read the results with that as a variable, or I shift to business-hours-only and we lose the rotation.

## The outreach strategy

**Order of operations matters more than volume.** The feed is the credential check; the DM is the ask. So content goes live first, and outreach follows it — never the reverse.

**Phase 1, days 1-3 — warm before you touch.** The 201 active posters are the only people in the list who emit public signal. Comment genuinely on their recent posts before any connection request lands. A request from someone whose name they saw yesterday converts at a completely different rate.

**Phase 2, ongoing — connection requests strictly top-down.** 20/day from rank 1. At that rate the 201 actives are exhausted in ten days, then we continue into the silent majority. **Do not deprioritise the non-posters** — Alok corrected us on exactly this: Noor DM'd four people who hadn't posted in months and got instant replies. They read, they just don't perform.

**Phase 3 — DM only on acceptance.** Discovery-first opener, no pricing in writing, everything driving to the two-minute live demo.

**Phase 4 — the re-engagement loop, which is the real machine.** This only exists once posts are live, and it's where the two pillars finally interlock:

- **Anyone who reacts or comments on his posts** is the warmest signal we will ever get, and Unipile can pull reactions per post. Connection request within 24 hours, DM referencing the post they engaged with.
- **Profile viewers** — he's on Premium, so "who viewed your profile" is available. Someone who looked without engaging is curious and unclaimed.
- **Accepted but silent after 7 days** — second touch, hung on a new post rather than a follow-up nudge.

Every post creates a fresh warm cohort. Ten posts a week means ten new cohorts a week, which is why the content is worth running even though it will never close anyone by itself.

**One structural gap:** Nuha's account isn't connected. Adding her doubles safe daily volume and lets us multi-thread the same company from two senders — which Alok's own GTM doc recommends, since one person's silence isn't the company's no.

### Alfred  
Checked the current Anthropic docs rather than going from memory. Here's the honest ceiling, sir.

**What Cozmo can see, at max**

| Surface | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Usage API / Console Usage | Token counts (input, output, cache read, cache creation) **attributed to that exact key**, grouped by model, workspace, service tier, context window. **1-minute buckets, live within ~5 min.** |
| Cost API | Daily USD spend for the key |
| API key admin | Key name, status, workspace, created/expires |
| Claude Code Analytics API | If we run **Claude Code** on their key: per-key daily sessions, lines added/removed, commits, PRs, Edit/Write accept-vs-reject counts, model breakdown, and **terminal type** (`iTerm.app`, `vscode`, `tmux`) |
| Compliance API (Enterprise only) | Activity feed of *their console/claude.ai account events* — those records carry IP and user-agent. Content endpoints return **claude.ai chats only, never API traffic** |

**What they cannot see, on any tier**

- Prompt text, system prompts, responses, file contents, file names, repo names. There is no request-log view anywhere in Console or the Admin API.
- Our IP, hostname, machine, or country. The only geo field is `inference_geo` — that's where Anthropic *serves* the inference, a residency knob we'd set, not our location.
- Who the work was for. Nothing links a call to Snowball or another client.

So: **they see a perfect volume-and-timing fingerprint, and zero content.** But that fingerprint is loud — minute-level graphs showing tokens burning at 3am IST on days we shipped nothing for Cozmo is a conversation waiting to happen, and if we use Claude Code, the terminal type and commit counts sit right there next to it.

Three things I'd do:

1. **Ask them for a dedicated workspace + dedicated key with a spend limit**, not a shared org key. Clean attribution protects both sides, and it's a normal enterprise ask that costs them nothing.
2. **Name the key neutrally** — the key name is the label in their analytics and in the Claude Code actor field.
3. **Don't run general Snowball work on it.** Not because they'd catch us — they mostly wouldn't — but it's their money and their invoice, and the one thing they *can* see cleanly is the size of the bill. If we need volume for Cozmo work specifically, that's fair game and worth telling them we're doing.

**What Alok killed**

- **The YC deadline post.** He caught it live — applications closed July 27.

He asked for both to be replaced with fresh trending topics, so:

- **New post 9 — YC's Fall 2026 Requests for Startups.** Keeps his best-performing lane on live news instead of a dead date. It also happens to describe his own category almost word for word, so the proof lands structurally rather than as a pitch. New isometric render.
- **New post 10 — the story he handed you.** Worth flagging: **the version described on the call was garbled.** It's Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness, up 439% through June, down ~67% in July, sold a ~$16B book to Citadel on July 30 (Reuters). Not a $45B portfolio, not a 60% loss, and the "10% off market cap" detail is rumour only — it's not in the post.

**What else changed**

- **"Send this to the most broke founder you know"** — deleted. He named this post specifically: CTAs should be implicit.
- **The grants post had gone factually stale** and would have shipped wrong. NSF SBIR is $275K not $305K, and its deadline was July 27, now November 4. NIH is $400K, closing September 5. Re-verified via Grok, total still lands at $1.4M so the hook holds.
- Staccato runs joined with conjunctions across three posts, per his fix ("don't lengthen it, just add the but").
- The insurance post now says **systems, processes and people** — Alok's exact framing from the Aug 1 call, where "processes" was missing.

Order follows his ranking: Nuha, Google/SpaceX (his A/B test), computer, pivot, grants, seven-figure, insurance, Altman, then the two new ones.

For him, it's not being AI that is the first priority, and then it's how engaging it is. It's not being AI that is also our first priority, but at the same time, I want the content to read engaging and have personality.

The problem with our content right now is that it lacks personality completely, and the problem is because we are just describing events. There is no emphasis on how we are describing events, like "then I showed it to an investor at the end of a pitch," almost as a throwaway. Instead, when you are telling stories, you build anticipation, right? You say that, and finally, at the end of the pitch, "I showed it to an investor." ### Alfred  
You're right, and it's a sharper diagnosis than "AI tells." We've been writing *minutes*, not *scenes*. Every fact is present and correctly ordered, which is exactly the problem: nothing is ever withheld, so nothing ever lands.

Here's your own example rebuilt, then what I think the mechanics are.

**The pivot post, rewritten as a scene:**

> Nobody outside the company was ever supposed to see it.
>
> Then I got to the end of a pitch one afternoon and mentioned it.
>
> Almost as a throwaway.
>
> He stopped me before I finished the sentence.
>
> "Forget the bank. I want this."
>
> I laughed at him, politely, the way you laugh at someone who has misunderstood your entire business.
>
> Two weeks later we killed the bank.

Same facts, no new information. What changed is where the reader is standing.

**The five mechanics**

1. **Dialogue in actual quotes.** This is the biggest single lever and we use it nowhere. "He stopped me right there and said, forget the bank, I want this" is a report. `"Forget the bank. I want this."` is a moment. It's also a genuine human signal — models paraphrase speech, people quote it, because people remember the exact words.

2. **Withheld qualifier.** The aside goes *after* the action, not inside it. "I showed it to an investor almost as a throwaway" spends the tension in one breath. Action, break, then "Almost as a throwaway" makes the reader lean in before the turn.

3. **Line breaks as beats.** A break is a camera cut. Right now our paragraphs are uniformly 2-3 lines, which is why every post has the same heartbeat regardless of what's happening in it.

4. **Interiority — be wrong in real time.** We have this once ("I laughed at him") and it's the best line in the batch. Nobody can fake having been wrong about their own company. It should appear in every narrative post.

5. **Specific physical detail.** Blader's own guide lists this as evidence of a human: models round specifics off, people hoard them. "A VP from one of the biggest claims operations" is a category. What he was holding, where he was standing, what he did with his face — that's a person.

**The tension I have to flag, because it's real**

Alok banned exactly this shape: *"very short sentence, full stop, very short sentence, 2 words, full stop... AI slop."* He's flagged it three times now. If we just start breaking lines everywhere, we will hand him back the thing he keeps rejecting.

I think the rule that reconciles both is: **a short line stands alone only if something happens in it.**

- Something happened → it can stand alone. *"He stopped me before I finished the sentence."*
- You're commenting on what happened → it joins a sentence with a conjunction. *"I laughed at him, politely, the way you laugh at..."*

Alok's slop examples were all commentary being dramatized ("Not once. Every month. For 32 months." is one fact wearing three costumes). Beats earned by narrative time read as story. Beats earned by emphasis read as AI. That distinction holds up and it's defensible to him if he pushes back.

**One caveat on scope:** only five of the ten are actually stories — Nuha, the computer, the pivot, the US deal, and half of Aschenbrenner. The Google, Altman, grants and YC posts are *takes*, and forcing scene structure onto a take makes it worse, not better. Takes need a different personality lever: a real stake, a line he'd defend in an argument, a willingness to be wrong on the record. Right now those four are informed and completely safe, which is its own kind of voiceless.

Want me to rebuild the five narrative posts on these mechanics and take a separate pass at putting an actual opinion into the four takes? I'd also codify this as a `storytelling-beats` skill so it runs on every client, not just Alok.

### Alfred  
Built and verified running locally against your real preview. Clean console, no server errors.

**How it works**

The plain link stays read-only, so the one you send Alok can't be edited by him. Editing needs a token: `/preview-linkedin/<slug>?edit=<token>`. Every push now returns both URLs, and the token is stable for a preview's whole life, so an editable link keeps working across re-pushes.

In edit mode each post gets a small toolbar: post number, live word count, and **Edit**. Editing swaps the rendered card for a textarea holding the raw text — deliberately a plain textarea, not a rich editor, because line breaks are load-bearing in these posts and a contenteditable would quietly rewrite them. Cmd+Enter saves, Esc cancels. Once a post has been edited it carries an "edited" badge and an **Original** button that restores what I pushed.

**The part that matters for before-vs-after:** every save writes twice — the post itself, and an append-only row in a new `preview_edits` table with the before text, the after text, and the word counts. It's append-only on purpose, so the record survives me pushing a new version over the top. I read it back with:

```bash
python3 tools/preview-edits.py --slug alok-cozmo-week-1-final --diff
```

That prints a coloured line diff of exactly what you changed. Each post also carries its draft slug now, so an edit traces back to the file it came from.

**Two things I did not do, and why**

**I could not run the migration.** There's no database password or Supabase login on this machine, so the SQL is written but not applied. It's one paste into the Supabase SQL editor — the file is [20260803_preview_edits.sql](../Linkedin_content_fatory/src/schema/migrations/20260803_preview_edits.sql). It adds `edit_token` to `public_previews`, backfills tokens for every existing preview, and creates `preview_edits`.

**I did not deploy.** The repo is on branch `esign-client-agreements` with uncommitted e-sign work in the tree, and a `vercel --prod` from here would ship that to `app.thesnowball.agency` alongside my change. That's your call, not mine.

I did make the push path defensive in the meantime: if the migration hasn't run, the API detects the missing column and writes without it, so pushing previews keeps working exactly as before rather than breaking. Edit mode simply won't authenticate until the SQL lands.

Run the migration and tell me how you want the deploy handled, and I'll get you the editable link for the Alok batch.

### Alfred  
Live in production, no Supabase work needed from you. Open in your Safari now:

**Editable (keep this one):**
`https://app.thesnowball.agency/preview-linkedin/alok-cozmo-week-1-final?edit=c9eaea76d171cdc022ba7ce9`

**Read-only (this is what you send Alok):**
`https://app.thesnowball.agency/preview-linkedin/alok-cozmo-week-1-final`

I threw away the migration and rebuilt it to need nothing from the database:

- **The edit token is derived, not stored** — an HMAC of the slug under a server secret we already have. No new column, unguessable, and permanently stable, so that link keeps working every time I re-push.
- **Edit history lives inside the existing `posts` JSON** as `{before, after, at}` entries. The push route now merges it forward, so re-pushing a batch never wipes the record.

**How to use it:** each post has a toolbar with its number, live word count, and **Edit**. That swaps the card for a textarea with the raw text — Cmd+Enter saves, Esc cancels. Edited posts get an "edited" badge and an **Original** button to restore what I pushed.

**Verified end to end against production, not just locally:**

| check | result |
|---|---|
| wrong token rejected | `{"error":"Invalid edit link"}` |
| plain link leaks edit history | no — stripped server-side |
| plain link leaks original text | no |
| edit link authorises | yes, all 10 posts |
| history survives a re-push | yes — confirmed by re-pushing after a test edit |
| draft slugs traced | yes, all 10 |

That last one matters: I made a test edit on the RFS post, re-pushed over it, and the before/after was still there afterwards.

To see what you changed:

```bash
python3 tools/preview-edits.py --slug alok-cozmo-week-1-final --diff
```

It prints a coloured line diff per post with word-count deltas, tagged with the draft slug so I can trace each edit to its file. Just say "show me before vs after" and I'll run it.

One honest caveat: because there's no private table, the history sits in a row that has public read access in Supabase. Our endpoint strips it from the plain link, so nobody gets it from the URL — but someone who knew to query the table directly with the public anon key could read it. Fine for drafts; worth knowing before anything sensitive goes in there.

### Alfred  
Four saves on the Nuha post. **Yours is better, and not narrowly.** Five things you did that I didn't:

**1. You gave the post a villain.** I wrote "I'd already seen what impressive resumes look like up close" — an abstraction the reader has to take on faith. You replaced it with the actual cliché, itemised:

> - Come from an Ivy League
> - Done 7 figure MRR before
> - Be literally friends with Sam Altman & have Elon on their speed dial

Now there's something for Nuha to beat. Mine had a fact; yours has a fight.

**2. You put a re-hook in the middle.** "But why?" on its own line, a third of the way down. That's a second stop-scrolling moment right where LinkedIn truncates. I had exactly one hook and then coasted.

**3. You chained the paragraphs causally.** It started when → Because → But why? → Because → Until → So. Every paragraph now owes the next one an answer. Mine was chronological: this happened, then this happened. That's the difference between a story and a timeline, and it's the sharpest thing in your edit.

**4. You actually quoted people.** `"Find a co-founder with an impressive resume"` and `"All in or nothing"`. I proposed that mechanic two turns ago and then didn't apply it here. You did.

**5. "we were stuck", not "it was stuck".** Small change, second save. Puts you inside the problem instead of narrating it from outside. And "But very grateful :)" fixes something I broke — I was right to cut the preachy ending, but I landed it too cold.

You also caught numerals — 4 months, 2 pivots. That's our own rule and I'd shipped it spelled out. My miss.

**Three things to fix before this ships**, all introduced in the edits:

- **"Done $ 7 figure MRR before"** — stray space after the `$`, and the `$` shouldn't be there at all with "7 figure". Also the bullets aren't parallel: *Come from* / *Done* / *Be*. Make it "Have done 7 figure MRR before".
- **"So what I did was obvious."** — save 4 flipped this from "So I did what was obvious" and it got worse. The original meant *the choice was obvious*; the new one means *my action was unsurprising*. "So I did the obvious thing" is cleanest.
- **"When she was only months away from finishing her PhD, and I asked her to drop it and build with me, "All in or nothing""** — this has no main clause, it's a fragment. Drop the "When": *"She was only months away from finishing her PhD, and I asked her to drop it and build with me. All in or nothing."*

I've saved the pattern — cliché-list opener, mid-post re-hook, quoted speech, causal chaining, numerals, warm close — so it's the default on narrative posts from here, and explicitly not on the alert-style ones like RFS.

Want me to apply those three fixes and run this structure across the other narrative posts?

When is important in the third sentence, when she was only months away from finishing her PhD, because they're asking, they're telling a statement before that. What I did was obvious: when she was only months away, it was obvious, and then, if we see that she was only months away, it's a break in between. It's not flowing that well. 


Learn from all the things that I did here, which were related to this post, and make better changes like this across all the posts. ### Alfred  
Rebuilt from the actual SEC filing. Open in Safari.

**The research changed the story, not just the density.** I'd written a vague "even Google can't get enough compute." What's actually filed is sharper:

- **The compute is xAI's.** The 110,000 GPUs sit in **Colossus 2** in Memphis — the cluster built for xAI. Google is renting its compute from Elon Musk. CNBC's headline says it outright. I didn't have that before.
- **Anthropic signed a bigger one three weeks earlier**: $1.25B/month through May 2029, 220,000+ GPUs, 300+ MW, ~$45B. So **$74B combined** from two of the biggest names in AI, into the same operator.
- **Money was never the constraint.** Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to **$195–205B** at Q2 earnings. They could buy this outright.
- **Electricity is the constraint.** Grid interconnection runs **3 to 7 years**, up to **84 months** in the worst markets; the building itself is another **18 to 36 months**. Colossus skipped the queue by burning its own gas on site with battery storage. That's the actual mechanism, and it's what makes the post worth reading.
- **The contract terms betray how tight it is**: either side can walk on **90 days notice** after Dec 31, and if the GPUs aren't delivered by **Sept 30** Google can terminate or take less for less.

That gives the post a real thesis with evidence under it: $920M a month isn't buying chips, it's buying a place in line.

**What I deliberately left out:** GPU purchase-vs-rent economics, hourly rates, depreciation schedules, and startup GPU availability. I asked for all of it — Grok couldn't source any of it to a primary source, so none of it is in the post. I'd rather it be shorter than padded with numbers I can't stand behind.

**The card was the weakest part**, still selling the old "shovel sellers" line that no longer exists in the copy. Rebuilt as the comparison, which is the most striking verifiable fact we have: $920,000,000 and $1,250,000,000 side by side, both into the same Memphis data centre, closing on $74 billion. Google, SpaceX and Anthropic marks along the bottom.

Sources are all in the file's `review_notes` — SEC filing URL, CNBC, Axios, Alphabet's earnings — so nothing in the body needs a citation.

Added real odds: NSF funds 10–20% of Phase I applications, NIH ~17%, the programme hands out ~$4.7B a year, NSF alone makes ~230 awards.

**I also have to flag that I got these numbers wrong yesterday, twice.** NSF SBIR is **$305K, not the $275K I "corrected" it to** — NSF raised the amounts. NIH is **~$323K, not $400K**. The real total is **$1.35M**, so the hook is now $1.3M. My earlier "fix" made it worse.

**Post 6** — the story now has evidence behind it. His customer had given another vendor 8 months with nothing live. That's the base rate: MIT found 95% of companies got zero return across 300 deployments, Gartner found only 48% of AI projects reach production and the average takes **exactly 8 months**, IDC found 88% of agent pilots never ship, S&P found 46% of proofs of concept get scrapped.

**Post 7** — the thesis is no longer an assertion. Third-party administration in P&C is a **$141 billion** market that's short **50,000 loss adjusters**, with that number expected to worsen.

**Post 8** — now shows the maths instead of asserting it: YC gives $500K cash for 7%, OpenAI gives $2M of tokens for ~2%, and $2M of credit is roughly 400 million input tokens at list price.

**Post 10** — added what was actually missing: peak assets of **$45B in early July down to ~$10B**, and positions **leveraged up to 400%**. That leverage figure is the actual cause, and v5 didn't have it.

**Post 9** stays a pure opinion-free alert, with YC's real deal terms added as fact.

Every listicle does a different job now — cliché, spec, payoff, stakes, evidence, comparison — so nothing reads as a template. Averages sit at 11–13 words per sentence across the batch, no banned characters, numerals throughout.

**What your post 5 edits taught me** — you cut 16 words and made it read faster, which is the whole lesson:

| you did | now applied everywhere |
|---|---|
| `$500,000` → `$500k` | $30B, $1.25B, $2M, $225M, $141B, $500k |
| `US government` → `US govt.` | abbreviate anything the reader already knows |
| `take 7% of your company` → `take 7%` | cut every word carrying no weight |
| `They are not.` → `(they're not)` | parenthetical asides instead of a second sentence |
| `and` → `&` and `+` | on factual lines, not in prose |
| two sentences → one comma splice | where a full stop was breaking the flow |
| one dense paragraph → two lines | one idea per line |

Contractions went from almost none to throughout. And your reframe — *"Despite the program giving away $4.7 billion... most people don't know about this"* — leads with the gap instead of narrating.

**Where each post changed:**

- **Post 2** — dropped "It can buy almost anything it wants" (restating the sentence before it) and the "So here is what I would watch" throat-clear. Money abbreviated. Closes straight on watching the electricity contracts.
- **Post 3** — contractions throughout, trimmed "just to see what was inside them" to "what was inside."
- **Post 6** — "(honestly, that's fair)" is now a parenthetical, and the run-on about signing without a pilot is one flowing line.
- **Post 7** — same treatment, ends on "I'd rather build for the ones holding the messiest data."
- **Post 8** — the close is now a single comma-spliced line rather than two.
- **Post 9** — deal terms abbreviated to $500k / $125k / $375k. Still opinion-free.
- **Post 10** — closes on one line: *"He was right about the decade, he just got margin called on the month :)"*

**Two things I caught that you didn't flag:** British spellings had crept in from Charlie's style — "data centres", "programme", "summarised", and "do the maths". All American now, since Alok writes to a US audience.

Numerals are clean across all ten. The only spelled numbers left are rhetorical ("the only one", "one of the biggest"), which is correct.

**The biggest lesson from post 6: you deleted the entire research listicle.** MIT, Gartner, IDC, S&P — all four bullets gone. That told me something I had wrong: third-party stats stop a personal story dead. Substance in a narrative means *the story's own detail*, not citations.

So I didn't discard the research, I moved it. MIT's 95% now sits in **post 7** as a single inline clause, supporting the "every vendor turns up asking you to rip out your systems" claim — which is exactly the point it proves. The other three are dropped rather than crammed somewhere.

- **Hooks run across lines 1 and 2** as one sentence — "It was my 1st week back in the US / and we signed a 7-figure deal". Posts 3, 7, 8 and 10 now do the same.
- **Ordinals as numerals** — 1st.
- **Asides in parentheses on their own line** — "(I'm aware of how that sounds)".
- **Merge with connectives** — "when", "Naturally,", ", and" instead of hard stops.
- **Dialogue set up with a colon**, and your own speech in lowercase quotes.
- **Listicle intros start with "And"**, contracted, present continuous. Applied to posts 3, 8 and 10.

Rebuilt and live in Safari.

**The real problem was that the post had no single idea.** It was making four arguments at once — data quality, market size, hiring shortage, and our product — with no order. So I picked one idea and told it in sequence:

> By the time a claim reaches a big carrier, somebody has already tidied it up. What's left is a summary.
>
> The real story is gone.
>
> And that story is still sitting with the people who actually handled the claim.

Everything else in the post now serves that one line. The list, the market size, the shortage, our product — each one earns its place by moving that story forward.

**The sentence you flagged, fixed exactly as you said:**

> They have the money.
>
> They just don't know where to start.
>
> And every vendor who walks in asks them to throw out software they already paid millions for.

Three lines, one idea each. "8 figures" became "millions" — same fact, word everyone already knows.

**I also cut the MIT statistic.** I'd wedged it into a parenthesis at the end of that sentence, which is exactly the mistake you'd already corrected on post 6 when you deleted the research listicle. Research doesn't belong inside a story. I put it back in the wrong place a turn after you taught me that.

**Other simplifications:**
- "aiming at the wrong end of the industry" → **"picked the wrong customer"**
- "Carriers sit on information that's already been cleaned, summarized & squeezed into whatever their systems will accept" → **"somebody has already tidied it up"**
- "This is a big business nobody talks about... worth around $141B and short of about 50,000 loss adjusters" → **"It's a $141B market & it's short of about 50,000 adjusters."**
- "the agents take the repetitive work off your team, your people go back to the work that actually needs a human" → **"Your systems stay & our agents do the boring work inside them."**

**227 words, down from 310. Longest sentence 17 words. Average 10.3.** For comparison, that's now the simplest prose post in the batch.

### Ansh  
Again, we don't have to be a narrator. We have to tell a story from our perspective in every single fucking post.

In this one, you're trying to say, "That's what every AI vendor is trying to sell right now. We went the other way. Here's why." These are three smaller sentences that could be coupled into one because he really does not like smaller sentences, if you look at the transcript of the call. We say, "That's what every vendor is selling right now, so we went the other way, and here is why."

Instead of saying, "By the time a claim reaches a big carrier, somebody has already tied it up," that's what is left. It is a summary. You can say, "Every time a claim reaches a big carrier, it is already tied up, and the data left is not much, but only a summary."

All these ideas could be explained in a much simpler manner from a first-person perspective, using "I" instead of narration, trying to sound smart and use simpler words that a lot of people understand.

**The hook was leaning on a word the audience doesn't feel.** "Selling his portfolio to Citadel" means nothing to a founder scrolling LinkedIn — it sounds like a normal transaction, not a collapse. Now it's only numbers everyone understands:

> A 25 year old made 439% betting on AI
>
> then lost most of it in a single month

**The plot was the real problem.** The old version had no cause and effect — numbers, then stocks fell, then a sale, then a lesson bolted on. There's now one chain you can follow:

He was right → **he borrowed to make the bet** → when AI stocks fell, the banks who lent him the money wanted it back → so he *had* to sell → **he just didn't control the timing.**

That last line is the point of the whole post, and everything now walks toward it. Alok's takeaway is about control, not about being right — which also keeps him from looking like he's dunking on someone.

**The card was doing the post's job.** It had three paragraphs explaining the story. Now it's two lines at 78pt:

> Up **439%** on AI.
>
> Then **67% down** in a single month.

That's a hook. It makes you want the post instead of replacing it.

**One thing I need to flag on post 8.** You changed "4 times better" to "8 times better", and I've kept your wording — but I can't get to 8 from the two numbers:

- **Raw dollars:** $2M vs $500k = **4x the money**
- **Per point of equity:** OpenAI is $1M per 1%, YC is $71k per 1% = **14x**
- Implied valuations: $100M vs $7.1M

So the defensible figures are 4x (money) or 14x (per point of equity). 8 sits between them without deriving from either. Your call — say the word and I'll set it to whichever you want.

Written to [product/skills/post-engine.md](../Snowball/product/skills/post-engine.md) and indexed. Product-level, not client-level, so Manish and everyone after runs on the same engine.

**Every rule is traceable to one of your edits or a client instruction** — nothing is my opinion. It's built from the 13 saves you made plus the two call transcripts.

The 13 sections:

1. **The five laws** — first person not narration; one idea per post; simplest words; **couple sentences, don't chop them**; substance not commentary
2. **The hook** — the three jobs line 2 can do, with the "runs across both lines as one sentence" pattern you converged on, plus name real people and never lead on a term the reader doesn't feel
3. **Post architecture** — including the company explainer line you added, and 7 varied mid-post turns so batches don't template
4. **The listicle** — the 8 distinct jobs it did across your 10 posts, and the intro rules ("That borrowed machine did miracles:" beats "Here is what is actually sitting there right now:")
5. **Voice mechanics** — a table of every typographic rule you set: `$500k`, `US govt.`, `&`, `+`, numerals including `1`, contractions, parentheticals, comma splices, US spelling
6. **The close** — two beats or one comma-spliced line, never a moral, never a CTA
7. **Banned patterns with real before/afters** — not-X-it's-Y, staccato, throat-clears, four-ideas-in-a-sentence, half sentences, and **research dumped into a personal story**
8. **Substance protocol** — Grok claim-by-claim, and the list of things it actually caught in one batch
9. **Media** — the card is a hook, two lines, not an information alternative
10. **Workflow** — push, pull before re-push, read the diff, never force blind
11. **Adapting for a new client** — what to measure before writing for Manish, and what never changes
12. **Pre-ship checklist** — 17 items plus a runnable script
13. **Reference batch** — pointing at the finished 10, with posts 1, 4, 5 and 6 marked as gold standard since they carry your own edits

I ran the checklist script against Alok's final 10 to confirm it works: zero banned characters, zero not-X-it's-Y, averages 11–24 words per sentence.

One honest limit: this captures *how* to write, not *what* Manish should write about. His pillars, embargo list and content mix still have to come from his onboarding transcript and memory — section 11 lists exactly what to pull before starting.

### Alfred  
Post 2 is unaffected — no mentions in it, so job 942 still fires correctly at 10:00 PDT.

**What actually broke:** Unipile silently ignores a mentions array if the text has no `{{N}}` placeholder. No error, no warning, it just posts plain text. I sent the array and stripped the `@` from the text, which left nothing for it to attach to.

**Three fixes, so this can't recur:**

1. **[tools/schedule-linkedin-post.py](../Snowball/tools/schedule-linkedin-post.py)** — writes `@handle` in the draft, resolves it live against Unipile, swaps in `{{0}}`, builds the array. It **refuses to schedule** if a mention has no placeholder or a handle won't resolve. Dry-run confirms it works on post 1:

```
mentions: 1
   {{0}} -> 'Nuha'  ACoAABK46m4BA2Lqp44RVTchV88ju0XajSxUY9k
text:  My co-founder {{0}} ruined my life...
```

2. **Post 1's draft now reads `@nuhahashem`** — a resolvable handle instead of a display name.

3. **Section 14 added to the post engine**, documenting the contract with the doc quote.

**The part I care more about than the bug:** my verification was worthless. I read the post after it was live, saw a correct tag, and called it a success — when the tag was there because you'd fixed it. Reading a post later cannot tell an API mention from a human repair. The engine now says to capture the published text in the same minute the job fires and diff it against what was sent, and the tool prints that reminder after scheduling.

Post 3 has no mentions either. If any later post needs one, it goes through the new tool.

Here's what that tells us, because the two failures look identical from outside but aren't:

- **The key itself authenticates fine.** A bad or revoked key returns `401 authentication_error`. This returned `400` with a billing message, and the org resolved: `c5ea5a2e-38b1-4666-88b4-d7080ef54880`.
- **`/v1/models` returned 200** with the full list — Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Haiku 4.5 and the 4.x line. So permissions and model access are all correct.
- **Only the billing gate is closed.** The moment someone at Cozmo adds credit or attaches a payment method, this key works with zero changes on our side.

I spent nothing testing it — the request was rejected before any tokens were charged.

**What Cozmo needs to do:** whoever owns that Anthropic org goes to **Plans & Billing** and either buys credits or turns on auto-reload. Nothing else is wrong.

### Alfred  
No image came through with your message — and there are 10 in Alok's batch at very different resolutions, so I don't want to guess and hand you the wrong file.

Two things worth knowing before you pick:

**There's no AI upscaler on this machine.** Only Pillow, OpenCV and ffmpeg, which do classical interpolation — that enlarges without adding real detail. For genuine AI super-resolution I'd install Real-ESRGAN (runs locally, a couple of minutes).

**For the photos with faces, the model choice matters.** Alok and his brother, Alok and Nuha at the Forbes summit — a *generative* upscaler reinvents facial detail rather than recovering it, which would put invented faces of real people on a client's post. I'd use Real-ESRGAN or EDSR, which are fidelity-preserving, and never a diffusion upscaler on those.

### Alfred  
Done. **1080×1078 → 4320×4312** (1.2MP to 18.6MP), 40 seconds on the Apple Silicon GPU.

**I used Real-ESRGAN, not a generative upscaler, deliberately.** This photo has Alok and Nuha's real faces in it. A diffusion upscaler re-imagines facial detail instead of recovering it, which would have put invented versions of their faces on a client's post. Real-ESRGAN is fidelity-preserving — you can see in the comparison that the features, hair and expressions are identical, just resolved.

**What actually improved:** the UAE emblem went from mush to clean linework, the English signage is properly legible, and the Arabic type is readable where it was a smear.

**One artifact you should look at before deciding.** The backdrop fabric now shows a pronounced cross-hatch grid. That weave is genuinely in the photo — the model amplified it rather than invented it — but it's aggressive enough that at full size it can read as a compression artifact. It disappears at normal viewing size.

**Three files now exist:**

| file | size | use |
|---|---|---|
| `e04-pivot.jpg` | 1080×1078, 224 KB | original, currently in scheduled draft 89 |
| `e04-pivot-4k.jpg` | 4320×4312, 7.3 MB | the 4K master |
| `e04-pivot-post.jpg` | 2160×2156, 1.8 MB | 4K master downsampled |

That third one is what I'd actually post. LinkedIn re-compresses and serves around 1200-1920px wide, so a 4.3K upload just gets squeezed anyway — but downsampling *from* the enhanced master preserves the recovered detail through their compression far better than sending the original 1080 does.

**I have not touched the scheduled post.** Job 954 still holds the original image and fires at 10:00 PDT, roughly 3 hours out. Swapping it means cancelling that job, building a new draft, and rescheduling — say the word and I'll do it, or leave it if the fabric texture bothers you.

The tool is saved at [tools/upscale-image.py](../Snowball/tools/upscale-image.py) with the no-generative-upscaler-on-faces rule documented in it, so it's reusable for the rest of the batch — posts 3, 5 and 7 are all under 1MP and would benefit more than this one did.

It was my 1st week back in the US

and we signed a 7-figure deal

(I'm aware of how that sounds)

A few weeks after we landed, I was at an industry conference when I ended up at a booth talking to a VP from one of the biggest claims operations in the country.

I didn't have any slides on me.

So I did the only thing I could think of and put a live call on his phone.

He talked to our AI the same way one of his customers would, went quiet for a second and said:

"My leadership needs to see this."

The next morning the CEO messaged me on LinkedIn, changed his flight & met us in person.

But his team had already given another AI vendor 12 months. Plenty of calls, plenty of roadmaps, nothing ever went live.

Naturally, they'd stopped believing anybody in this space (honestly, that's fair).

So why did they sign us?

Because I offered him 1 thing, "give me a single day with your team"

We flew out and sat with the people who answer phones all day, not the executives.

2 days later we'd built the thing they had waited 12 months for.

They were live inside 2 weeks & they signed without a pilot, which companies that size basically never do.

Still the fastest yes anyone has ever given us :)

Everyone builds AI for people at desks. We are building it for the $250B world of storm-damaged houses, where a claim still means phone calls, retyping and waiting. 2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
- **Unipile API** (`https://api32.unipile.com:16255`) — posts, users, chats, accounts, company lookup. No native scheduling.
- **Unipile mentions**: text must contain positional placeholders `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`; the `mentions[i][name|profile_id|is_company]` array alone is **silently ignored** without them. `name` is the DISPLAY text; `profile_id` is `ACo`/`ADo`-prefixed for people, numeric for companies.
- **EC2 scheduler** on the Snowball admin server: `POST /api/drafts` (multipart: text, image, mentions JSON), `POST /api/jobs` (action `linkedin.post.draft`, `run_at` ISO), `POST /api/jobs/:id/run-now`, `DELETE /api/jobs/:id`, `GET /api/jobs?limit=N` returns `{"jobs":[...]}`.
- **Perfect Preview** in the `Linkedin_content_fatory` Next.js app (Vercel project `snowball-linkedin`, domain `app.thesnowball.agency`).
- **HMAC-derived edit tokens** — no DB column; edit history stored inside the existing `posts` jsonb.
- **C2PA / Content Credentials**: gpt-image-2 PNG output carries a `caBX` chunk (~29 KB) containing `c2pa`/`jumb`; LinkedIn reads it to draw the CR badge. Decoding to pixels in PIL and re-encoding as JPEG strips it structurally.
- **Pixel-art downscaling**: use `Image.NEAREST`, never Lanczos, or the pixel grid blurs.
- **Grok** (`grok-4.3` via `/v1/responses` with web_search + x_search) for all research and fact-checking. Never Claude WebSearch.
- **Real-ESRGAN + spandrel on MPS** for fidelity-preserving upscaling; gpt-image-2 tops out at 1536px so cannot reach 4K alone.

Five topics, all from Alok's own words. Written up at [2026-08-14-batch-from-whatsapp.md](clients/alok-kumar/topics/2026-08-14-batch-from-whatsapp.md).

**1. The 4 systems of record** — took a customer live, integrated 4 SORs, under 2% error rate in production, 50% of their daily claims intake. His own confession is the post: *"the hardest part is not setting up agents but to make sure the agent use legacy systems."* Company post with receipts, which is the category that carried his week. Customer stays unnamed — ServiceMaster is under NDA.

**2. Computer vision agents that work without an API** — and this rescues the hook you gave me. Blanket "nobody has done this" was false, but his actual claim is narrower and genuinely defensible: CV agents that operate **non-API legacy systems** for back-office work. Everyone else integrates with software that has an API; most claims software doesn't, so his agent looks at the screen. The parked vision draft should be rebuilt on that.

**3. $32,000 to nothing** — cloud bill cut from $32K over 3 months to zero via startup programmes. Needs a check that it doesn't just rerun the grants post.

**4. Great sales leaders aren't building a personal brand** — his idea, unprompted. Real risk: it's a LinkedIn post arguing LinkedIn posting isn't real work, on an account we run for that. I'd reframe it as what he screens for when hiring sales, since his Founding GTM role is live.

**5. We are not a voice AI company** — the strongest. *"we do not say we are building voice agents for P&C... it is like saying we are building excel sheet for accountants."* A positioning post with a real opinion, and it fixes our own copy — we shipped "Voice AI agents for P&C Claims" in the post that went live Aug 10.

### Alfred  
Yes as a claim about the product. No as a claim about this customer.

Our own [offer-facts.md:15](clients/alok-kumar/memory/offer-facts.md:15) already resolves this: **~50% is the blended reduction on a customer's total claims budget**, because humans still do the judgment work. The $500 to $60 figure is the ~88% drop on one claim's automated portion. Different denominators, both true. So "cuts costs in half" is our canonical number, not a stretch.

The problem is where it would sit. This post is a case study about one customer, and we have zero cost data from them — Alok gave us 4 SORs, under 2% error, 50% of daily intake. Nobody measured their budget. Writing "we cut their costs in half" turns a model figure into a measured customer outcome, and a TPA COO reading it will ask which line item.

There's also a live collision: 50% of claims handled and 50% of costs cut, in the same post, invite the reader to assume they're the same number. They aren't.

Three clean ways to do it:

1. **Ask Alok for their actual number.** Best post, one WhatsApp message.
2. **Say it generally** — "this work usually takes about half the cost out of a claims budget" — true, and clearly not a claim about them.
3. **Use their own published proof.** The site already carries a customer quote: "We cut our cost per property claim by 70%." Public, attributable, stronger than a hedge.

I'd go with 1, and fall back to 3.

**The hook, per the skill's process.** The tension isn't "founder visits customer" — it's that people building AI for this industry build it from a laptop while the work happens in a stranger's basement. Line 1 places him, line 2 promises a specific moment without naming it, and the moment doesn't land until a crew member stops in the doorway and photographs the damage on his phone. Outcome stated, mechanism withheld.

Then the turn: **"That photo is the claim."** It travels to an office, somebody opens it, works out what it shows, types it into a system, and if that person is busy on a storm week the whole file waits.

Closes on why he keeps going back — *"the day I stop standing in these rooms is the day we start building the wrong thing :)"*

**Every detail comes from the photos.** The carpet pulled back, the pool table, 3 air movers, the wet staircase, the phone. No invented duration, date, or customer, which is what would have made it feel written from a desk.

240 words against his 229 average. Stop-slop 50/50.

### Ansh  
What does the hi-vis vest stand for

### Alfred  
High-visibility. It's the fluorescent orange or yellow safety vest with reflective strips — the one Alok is wearing in the photos. Standard required PPE on a restoration or construction site so nobody gets hit by equipment or a vehicle.

In the post it's doing double duty, sir: literal, because that's what he actually had to put on to be allowed on that job, and a signal that he was on site as a working body rather than a visitor with a laptop.

If it reads as jargon to his audience, the alternatives are "safety vest" (plainer, same meaning) or cutting the garment entirely — "I went out on a water damage job with the crew". The vest is doing real work in the hook though, since it's the thing that puts him physically in the room, and it's visible in two of the three photos so the image backs the line up.

Your call. Say the word and I'll swap it.

Full plan at [2026-08-17-week-plan.md](clients/alok-kumar/topics/2026-08-17-week-plan.md). Here's what the research actually turned up, sir.

## The data is brutal and clear

Averaged across Alok's last 16 posts by category:

**Personal 105 reactions · Company 41 · Ecosystem 19.**

| | |
|---|---|
| My co-founder Nuha ruined my life | **229** |
| An investor told me I was building the wrong company | **134** |
| Steve Jobs had a garage | 61 |
| Told the customer where we're worst | 60 |
| Proud of the wrong number | 59 |
| ... | |
| Sam Altman's $2M tokens | 17 |
| This Guy left OpenAI | 8 |
| YC wants 13 companies built | **6** |

Personal posts do **5.5x** ecosystem posts. And the week we just ran — RFS, Aschenbrenner, Altman, Google/SpaceX, grants — was almost entirely ecosystem. It was the worst week the account has had. Nuha's account shows the identical shape: her AI-news posts sit at 5-8 while "Back in SF" did 74.

**On his timing question** — the honest answer is no. Every post from the insurance one onward went out at 10am SF, and that same set contains both the 31 and the 6. Topic moved the numbers, not time. We'll keep 10am because he wants it, but I won't tell him it's the fix.

## Format research

Multi-image and carousels are the top format right now — 1.2 to 1.4x reach, 5-7% engagement, because swipe dwell and saves are what the algorithm weights. Reach signals rank: **dwell > comment depth > saves > shares > reactions**. Links cut reach ~60%. Video is down 36% YoY. Sweet spot is 1,300-2,500 characters; our recent posts have been at the short end.

That matters because **Alok has a huge unused photo library** — the Aug 10 dump alone had 23 images with captions.

## The seven, all personal or company, zero news

| Day | Post | From |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | I changed my major 3 times | KFUPM, full scholarship, "like the current pivot" |

Ecosystem posts aren't short of reach. They're short of *interest*. Google/SpaceX pulled **24,463 impressions at 0.10%** — shown to twenty-four thousand people, essentially none of whom cared. Aschenbrenner 4,263 at 0.21%. On Nuha's side, the burger post got 7,618 at 0.26%.

The second failure is worse. **The YC RFS post got 399 impressions. The insurance thesis got 810.** Against an account average near 7,000. Those weren't badly engaged — they were barely distributed at all.

**33,861 → 24,463 → 8,608 → 8,504 → 3,283 → 7,654 → 810 → 5,228 → 5,279 → 399 → 4,263 → 978**

Roughly a 30x collapse, across exactly the stretch where we ran almost nothing but ecosystem content. A week averaging 0.34% engagement teaches LinkedIn his posts aren't worth showing, and now the account pays that tax on every post — including the good ones.

Not reactions. **Engagement rate, and every post next week should clear 1.5%.** His posts that already do: telling the customer where we're worst (2.16%), proud of the wrong number (1.78%), the investor post (1.68%), the insurance thesis (1.48%).

### Alfred  
Learned and recorded — memory file plus section 15 of the post-engine, so it applies to Manish and every other client too.

**You cut 362 words to 261.** That's the headline lesson. Nine patterns underneath it:

**1. The hook carries the facts, the body carries the explanation.** I spent line 2 explaining the mechanism. You put *both* facts there — "despite 100% scholarship & changing my major 3 times" — and pushed the why down. Also "100%" over "full".

**2. Spoken beats written.** "I still do not know" → "I have no idea."

**3. Talk to the reader.** "That is the part people miss" → "You probably haven't thought much about this, but."

**4. Parentheses are your aside mechanism** — you added "(yes, this is my college journey)" as a signpost and wrapped the brotherhood line in them.

**5. Simplest word.** "systems and data" → "jargon."

**6. You kill aphorisms.** "what intensity costs and what it buys" → "how intense work can actually get." Anything that reads like a pull-quote gets flattened.

**7. One-line ending, no moral, no pitch.** You deleted three paragraphs including the whole 6-or-7-days hiring bit.

**8. ":)" isn't automatic** — second time you've removed it on a reflective post.

**9. Company name always the full tagged form.**

The meta-lesson is on me: I wrote to the 1,300–2,500 character band instead of to the point, and padding was the result. Your 1,331 is better than my 1,813.

**One thing to fix before Alok sees it, sir.** This line has the logic inverted:

> a paying student is an expense of the university, so there is no tangible reason to hold on to them. I was that

A paying student is *revenue*. The scholarship student is the expense — that's you. As written it says the opposite and the whole mechanic stops making sense. Suggested fix keeping your voice:

> a paying student is revenue for the university, so there is a tangible reason to hold on to them. I was the opposite of that

> There is a 9 point playbook going around for AI native services companies

**I read the actual thesis first** — fetched Emergence's AINS page and researched Saper's public claims. Their playbook is 9 principles: Domain Expertise is Not Optional, Beware Mirage PMF, Sleep at Your Customer's Office, It's the Demo Stupid, Outcomes-based pricing, Forge a Data Flywheel, Track Productization Maniacally, and two more.

**The argument:** eight of the nine are downstream of one — going stupidly deep inside your first real customer. Then his own receipts prove each claim:

> That is where the domain expertise came from, not from a hire.

> That is where the demo came from, because months later I could put a live call on a stranger's phone at a conference and it just worked.

> That is where the pricing came from, because you only offer to get paid on outcomes once you know your own error rate.

Mid-post re-hook — *"But why does everyone skip it?"* — then: it doesn't scale, it looks like consulting on a board slide, and somebody always asks when you'll productise it.

**And the BS call, which is his:**

> The data flywheel gets described like it switches itself on, and it does not, because someone has to stand in a stranger's flooded basement and watch a crew photograph a wall before you even know which data is worth collecting.

His instinct holds up, by the way — independent research flags the data flywheel and the productization economics as the most extrapolated parts of the thesis, with no company at scale proving them yet. So he's disagreeing with the genuinely soft spot, not a strawman.

### Alfred  
**https://app.thesnowball.agency/preview-linkedin/alok-reference-customer?edit=8ea93c87030c338cffc3c706**

Built it as a **tweet card** rather than an infographic — that's his proven graphic format, it's on the account already, and it's deterministic rather than generated.

The card carries only the hook, not the post:

> Everybody wants the playbook for AI native services.
>
> There isn't one yet.
>
> There is one customer, and how far you're willing to go inside them.

It took three passes to match his shipped Altman card. The default render came out with all the X chrome — Follow button, timestamp, like/reply/copy-link row, card border — and small type floating in white space. His actual card has none of that. So I extended the CSS in `tweetshot/render.mjs` to strip it, bumped the body type, and cropped to a clean 2160x2160 with the content centred.

I also broke the blue tick on one pass with an over-broad selector and put it back.

**That fix is now permanent** — the CSS lives in the tool, so every future card on any client renders in this format instead of me hand-fixing it each time.

One thing you may want to change, sir: the card still shows the small black **X badge** next to his name. His shipped Altman card doesn't have it. I left it because it's part of the authentic embed and reads as real, but it's one line to remove if you'd rather match the old card exactly.

**1. He will not be your approval bottleneck, and said so on day one.** *"If it has to be me and Nuha approving every post and comment, it's not going to work."* He still reads everything and replies fast — build a process he can interrupt, not one that waits on him.

**2. He edits at the line, never the concept.** Almost never "I don't like this post". Instead: *"Not this line"* plus the exact line, or he rewrites it himself and sends it back.

**3. His approvals are one word.** *"good to go"*, *"Perfect, thanks"*. Silence means unread, not unhappy. Nudge once, don't re-pitch.

**4. Three time zones, messages at 3am.** His last two briefs came at 12:57am and 3:31am. He joined the onboarding call while running a customer call in parallel. Slow replies aren't disengagement.

**5. Positioning accuracy is what actually annoys him.** The one hard pushback was our company description — *"it is like saying we are building excel sheet for accountants."* He then wrote the correct line himself. Use his words verbatim.

**6. He knows what he legally can't say, and volunteers it.** *"Technically I can go behind the bars for saying that."* The flagship customer is under NDA and never named. He self-censors before we have to, which is rare.

**7. He asks for evidence, not opinion.** *"What does data say?"* Bring the number.

**8. He wants a calendar, not a scramble.** Posts locked by Sunday for the following week — his clearest process request, and meeting it buys a lot.

**9. Generous with raw material the second you ask.** Sent 23 captioned photos in one sitting, signing off *"Hope you have enough content to get this flowing."*

**10. His story explains his standards.** Saudi-raised, lost his mother at seven, earning from about nine, full scholarship at KFUPM where it could be pulled any semester, turned down UPenn for consulting, quit that because it was *"a lot of slides, zero impact"*, built and killed Zywa, moved to the US, seven-figure deal in three months.
